title: The whirlpool ahead
hook: a man swept downstream, warned by someone on the bank

segments.voice: Yesterday: conscience and concern, and your line, listen to the small don't. Did you listen to one small don't? Today, a warning from outside, shouted from a riverbank. Day six hundred thirty-one.

A lazy river on a summer afternoon. Warm water, sun overhead, the current doing all the work. Nobody in the water has to decide anything. That's the picture at the start of a teaching near the end of the Itivuttaka. A man is being carried along by a river that looks lovely and pleasant. He's enjoying it. And then someone standing on the bank, someone who can see further down than he can, starts shouting. Today: the whirlpool ahead.
screen: `A LAZY RIVER, A SUMMER AFTERNOON.` → `THE CURRENT DOES THE WORK.` → `SOMEONE ON THE BANK SHOUTS.`

segments.voice: Hey, the man on the bank calls. You're being carried along by a river that looks pleasant. But downstream there's a pool with waves and whirlpools, with dangerous creatures in it. If you reach it, you'll come to grief. And the man in the water, hearing that, struggles against the current with his hands and feet. Then the Buddha explains the picture, piece by piece. The river's current is craving. The pleasant, alluring look of it is your own six senses, how good it all seems through them. The pool downstream stands for the five lower fetters, the ties that bind beings to this world. The waves are anger and despair. The whirlpools are the five strands of sense pleasure, the pull of sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches. Turning against the stream is renunciation. Struggling with hands and feet is effort. And the one standing on the bank, who can see what the swimmer can't? That, the Buddha says, is the one who has awakened. You may remember a swimmer from earlier this year, with four dangers in the water: waves, crocodiles, whirlpools, sharks. Today the river adds something: the danger doesn't look dangerous. It looks like a nice afternoon. That's why the warning matters. In the picture, the whirlpool can't be seen from the water; it takes someone on the bank. And the swimmer in the story hears, and turns.
screen: `A RIVER THAT LOOKS PLEASANT.` · `A POOL WITH WAVES AND WHIRLPOOLS.` · `THE CURRENT IS CRAVING.` · `THE ONE ON THE BANK CAN SEE.` · then, large: `THE WHIRLPOOL AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: heed one warning. Sit and settle. Think of a warning someone has given you lately, gently or not: a friend, a doctor, a parent, even your own body. Maybe you nodded and kept floating. Picture them on the bank, calling. What can they see that you can't from the water? You don't have to swim hard yet. Just turn your head toward the bank and listen. The bell holds the time.
Avatta, a whirlpool. In the Itivuttaka, a man carried by a pleasant river is warned from the bank of the whirlpools downstream, and turns. Today's word.
Your line: a stroke toward the bank. Today, take one warning seriously that you've been floating past, and make it. Day six hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use river and flood images for craving, and some describe the teacher's role, as here, as someone on the bank who can see dangers the practitioner cannot yet see.

fork.setup: you're floating down a lovely river. someone on the bank shouts that there are whirlpools ahead. what does the man in the Itivuttaka do?
options: struggle against the current with hands and feet.
fork.reveal: he hears and turns, working against the current. the Buddha says that struggle is effort, and the one on the bank is the awakened one.

original.note: Pali avatta: a whirlpool, an eddy. in Itivuttaka 109 the whirlpools are the five strands of sense pleasure.

trapdoor: what you thought: danger always looks dangerous.
what it means: the river looks pleasant; you need someone on the bank to see the whirlpool you can't.
what a scholar hears: Iti 109 (Nadisota Sutta) glosses each element of the simile, and the image parallels the swimmer's dangers of MN 67.

notes: Itivuttaka 109 paraphrased. The text also explains the dangerous creatures (crocodiles and demons) as standing for women; this element was left out of the voice and games. A Keeper should decide whether to address it.

Confirm the glosses: current = craving; pleasant look = six internal sense bases; pool = five lower fetters; waves = anger and despair; whirlpools = five strands of sense pleasure; effort; the man on the bank = the Tathagata.
Callback to day 459 (four dangers for a swimmer, MN 67).

Reviewer: the teach had folded 'against the stream' (renunciation) and 'struggling with hands and feet' (effort) into one gloss, and glossed the pleasant look as 'the six senses and their world'; both now follow the text's separate glosses (six internal sense bases; five lower fetters). Confirm.

Editor review (y2 614-631): hook no longer opens with a superlative ('one of life's easy pleasures') in second person; the simile's logic is kept inside the picture rather than stated as narrator fact; cut the stock 'the one thing that counts'; 'many describe' softened.
